You link ideas like an advanced speaker with connectors: for adding (además, incluso), for contrast (sin embargo, aun así, en cambio), for cause and consequence (ya que, por lo tanto, así que), for ordering (en primer lugar, por último).

I miss Madrid; however, I’m happy here.

To add ideas: además, incluso, también, no solo… sino también.
To contrast ideas: pero, sin embargo, aun así, en cambio, a pesar de (que).
To express cause and consequence: porque, ya que, como, por lo tanto, así que.
To organise a text: en primer lugar, por un lado, por último, en resumen.
To write a short, well-structured article.
A Spanish magazine for expats has asked Ana for an article: “What it’s like to live in Romania”. Ana is writing; Mihai reads over her shoulder.
Badly. I have lots of ideas, but they read like a shopping list. Listen: “Romania is beautiful. The people are friendly. The food is good. It’s cold.”
Ha-ha. You need connectors. For example: “Romania is a gorgeous country; moreover, the people are very friendly.”
OK. “However, it’s very cold in winter.” Like that?
Perfect. And you can add: “Even so, the houses are always warm, since the heating is very strong.”
That’s true. In Madrid, on the other hand, houses are cold in winter and like an oven in summer.
See? You’re already comparing. And what will you say about the language?
That Romanian is similar to Spanish; therefore, you understand lots of words. However, the pronunciation is very hard. In fact, I still can’t say “înghețată” properly.
Nobody can say it properly. Not even Romanians. And are you going to write about us?
A little. I’ll explain that, although I miss my family, here I’ve found another one. That is, yours. And Mrs Maria’s. And Mr Ilie’s.
Very nice. And how will you finish?
“In short: Romania isn’t an easy country. However, if you give it a chance, it pays you back tenfold.” What do you think?
I think you don’t need my help any more. So I’m off to change the baby’s nappy, because she’s been protesting for ten minutes.
seen-em-BAR-go: a little pause afterwards, marked by a comma in writing. «Sin embargo, | hace frío.»
a-de-MAS: stress on the last syllable. It often goes at the start: «Además, …».
The Romanian sounds â/î and ă don’t exist in Spanish. Ana says “in-ghe-TSA-ta”. You have the same problem with Spanish “rr” or “j”, just the other way round!
1. Adding: además, incluso, no solo… sino también
Aquí todos hablan inglés, incluso los abuelos.
No solo es bonita, sino también barata.
“No solo… SINO también” (not “pero también”). “Sino” is used after a negative: No es español, sino rumano.
2. Contrasting: sin embargo, aun así, en cambio
Él habla rumano; yo, en cambio, no.
a pesar de que / aunque + verb
A pesar de que hacía frío, salimos.
“Sin embargo” usually goes at the start of a new sentence, after a full stop or semicolon, and is followed by a comma.
Llueve; por lo tanto, no salgo.
“Como” meaning “as / since” goes at the START of the sentence: Como estaba cansada, me acosté. NOT “Me acosté como estaba cansada” (that would mean “as if”).
“Ya que” can also mean “since… anyway”: Ya que estás aquí, ayúdame (Since you’re here, help me).
en primer lugar → en segundo lugar → por último
en resumen, en conclusión, en definitiva
In a B1 exam, connectors earn lots of points in the writing paper. A text with 5–6 varied connectors shows your level straight away.
5. How to build a short article
The classic structure, with the connectors in place:
Mucha gente me pregunta…, Hoy quiero hablar de…
Por lo tanto estás aquí, ayúdame.
I miss my family; however, I’m happy here.
She was tired, so she went to bed.
Despite the cold, we went out for a walk.

The final version of Ana’s article, published in the magazine for Spaniards abroad.
Lots of people ask me why a woman from Madrid decided to live in Bucharest. The answer is simple: for love. However, I stayed for many other reasons.
First of all, the people. At first they seem serious, even a little cold. Even so, as soon as you get to know them, they invite you home and won’t let you leave without having eaten three courses.
Secondly, the language. Romanian is a Latin language; therefore, a Spaniard understands much more than they imagine. Speaking it, mind you, is another story.
On the one hand, I miss the Madrid sunshine, the terraces and dinner at ten. On the other, here I’ve discovered the pleasure of having dinner at seven and going to bed at a normal time.
In fact, my daughter was born here, in a hospital where the window was opened for ten seconds so she could breathe the city air. That is, part of me will always be Romanian now.
In short: Romania isn’t an easy country. However, if you give it a chance, it pays you back tenfold. And on top of that, it feeds you.
El placer de cenar a las siete
The move was on the last Saturday in May. In theory, it should have been simple: a few boxes, a few pieces of furniture and a twenty-minute drive. In practice, though, it turned into a party.

First of all, because the club from Madrid decided to come. Not everyone, of course; nevertheless, Hanako, Carlos and Sofía came, with three suitcases, a guitar and a jamón sent by Carmen “just in case”.

Secondly, because Mrs Maria had told the whole neighbourhood. Since in Bucharest nobody misses someone else’s move, by nine in the morning there were already twelve neighbours outside the house, offering help, advice and, above all, opinions.

Mr Ilie arrived at nine sharp in his van. He looked at the boxes, he looked at the neighbours and he looked at the Spaniards. He didn’t say anything. Even so, everyone understood that he was in charge.

For two hours, Mr Ilie organised everyone with gestures. The neighbours carried the heavy furniture. Carlos and Sofía, on the other hand, dealt with the small boxes, because Mr Ilie had decided that foreigners don’t know how to carry big things.

Hanako, for her part, had been given the most important mission: looking after Rosa Elena. She had taken her into the yard, where the baby was watching Mrs Maria’s six cats very attentively, and they, in turn, were watching her.

At midday the first problem appeared. Grandpa Gheorghe’s cradle wouldn’t fit through the door of the room with the balcony. The neighbours gave ten different opinions. One suggested taking the door off; another, taking the cradle apart; a third even suggested putting it in through the window.
Mihai, however, refused to take it apart. The cradle was made from a single piece of walnut, and Grandpa had worked for months carving it. Therefore, nobody was going to touch it.

In the end, it was Mr Ilie who solved the problem, as usual. He studied the door for five minutes, took a screwdriver out of his pocket and removed the frame so carefully that, an hour later, nobody would have said it had been touched.

Meanwhile, something extraordinary was happening in the kitchen. Sofía and Mrs Maria, who didn’t have a single word in common, had started cooking together. Sofía was making pasta. Mrs Maria was making mămăligă. And somehow they had decided to combine them.

The result was a kind of lasagne with layers of mămăligă, sheep’s cheese and tomato sauce. Carlos tasted it, closed his eyes and said it was the best thing he had ever eaten. In fact, he had three plates.

In the afternoon, when everything was in its place, Carlos took out the guitar. At first only he played. Little by little, though, the neighbours began singing Romanian songs, and the Spaniards tried to follow them without knowing the words.

Ana sat on the freshly painted balcony with a glass of wine in her hand and looked at the yard. There were cats, neighbours, friends from Madrid, a baby asleep in the arms of a Japanese woman, and a very serious man who, in spite of everything, was tapping his foot to the music.
Mihai sat down next to her.
“That a year ago I didn’t even know where this house was. And now it’s ours.”
“It isn’t only ours,” Mihai answered. “It’s Grandma Ileana’s, Grandpa Vasile’s, Mrs Maria’s, who looked after it, and Mr Ilie’s, who repaired it. We, on the other hand, are just going to live in it.”
“So we’re the tenants of a house with a lot of history.”
“Exactly. And, on top of that, without paying rent.”
That night, after everyone had left, the house was quiet for the first time. Ana put Rosa Elena to bed in the cradle, in the room where her grandmother Elena had been born.
Before turning off the light, she stood for a moment looking at her daughter. She was tired, her back ached and her hands were covered in dust. Even so, she had never felt so at home.

The scent of the neighbourhood’s acacias came in through the window. Downstairs, in the living room, under the floorboards, a wooden box silently kept three generations of stories. And in the cradle, the fourth was beginning.

The next morning, Ana woke up to a strange noise at the door. It was seven. She went downstairs in her pyjamas, with the baby in her arms, and opened it. There was nobody there. However, on the ground there was a basket.
Inside were fresh bread, a jar of cherry preserve, a bottle of milk and a note written in Spanish full of mistakes: “Welcome to the street. The neighbours.”
Ana stood looking at the basket for a long time. Then she went upstairs, woke Mihai and showed him the note.
“Did Mrs Maria write it?” he asked, half asleep.
“I don’t think so. Mrs Maria can’t write in Spanish. And besides, look at the handwriting: it’s a child’s. Or a teenager’s.”
Mihai looked at the note more closely. In the bottom corner, very small, there was a drawing: a white cat in a Mexican sombrero.
“Andrei,” they both said at the same time.
Apparently, the quiet boy from group C lived three streets down. And, also apparently, he had decided that his teacher was no longer a foreigner, but just another neighbour.
Ana put the note in the wooden box under the floor. It seemed to her that it belonged exactly there.
